panels.rationale: Single clinical photo of painful left ear in article titled Acute Auricular Perichondritis With an Effusion; caption states swelling of pinna with mild erythema and in-text states tender fluctuant swelling, supporting perichondritis with lobule sparing visible.
panels.attribution_text: Usoro and Ehmann. Acute Auricular Perichondritis With an Effusion.. Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine 2019. doi:10.5811/cpcem.2019.9.43947. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure Image 1.
panels.figure_caption: Photograph image of the left ear demonstrating swelling of the pinna (arrow) with mild overlying erythema.
in_text_mentions: A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department with one day of painful left ear swelling. He denied preceding trauma or recent instrumentation, but expressed concern that he might have been bitten by a spider while cleaning cobwebs in his basement two days prior. He denied systemic symptoms. The area of swelling was tender and fluctuant with mild overlying erythema (Image 1). Point-of-care ultrasound revealed an avascular anechoic fluid collection within the cartilaginous layer of the ear (Image 2).

panels.rationale: Single clinical photo of left auricle showing fluctuant anterior swelling with loss of normal contour, explicitly captioned as auricular hematoma in article titled recurrent auricular haematoma. Matches configured disease and vocabulary finding.
panels.attribution_text: Alsaqr et al. Recurrent auricular haematoma following nocturnal headphone compression: a case report.. Journal of surgical case reports 2026. doi:10.1093/jscr/rjag502. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Initial presentation demonstrating a fluctuant swelling involving the anterior aspect of the auricle, consistent with auricular hematoma, with associated erythema and distortion of the normal auricular contour.
in_text_mentions: On clinical examination, a localized, fluctuant swelling measuring ~2 × 2 cm was noted over the left auricle (Fig. 1). The overlying skin was intact, with no evidence of erythema or discharge. No other palpable swellings were noted, and no regional lymphadenopathy was identified. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory investigations demonstrated a mildly elevated C-reactive protein level of 7.1 mg/L, with no evidence of leukocytosis.
